vigor_pct: 55-65% of seedling; comparable to MM.106 or M.7, and 67-89% larger than M.26 EMLA in NC-140 trials
anchorage: free-standing; deep root system, does not require support per WSU, though some suckering is reported
disease_notes: Resistant to fireblight (Erwinia amylovora), Phytophthora crown rot, AND woolly apple aphid — the only stock in this set resistant to all three. Also tolerant of replant disease and rated winter hardy by WSU.
description: A Cornell/Geneva semi-vigorous rootstock producing a tree about MM.106 or M.7 size but markedly more yield-efficient, with the highest cumulative yields of any stock by a wide margin when NC-140 pooled thirteen locations. Its triple disease resistance plus deep anchorage make it the strongest choice in this set for an unsupported, wider-spaced maritime PNW cider orchard, and it performs notably well in harsh replant ground. It is the clear substitute for EMLA 106 anywhere drainage is marginal, and the right pairing for the fireblight-sensitive Amere de Berthcourt.
discrepancies: Two conflicts. Vigor is reported as 50-60% of seedling (Roots to Fruits), 60-70% (NMSU Extension), and as similar to EMLA 106 or M.7 (Cornell, Adams County); NC-140 trial data puts it 67-89% larger than M.26 EMLA. Recommended 55-65% as the range consistent with the trial data and the MM.106/M.7 size anchor, rather than either single nursery figure. Precocity is the sharper conflict: WSU's rootstock page calls G.890 intermediate precocity, while Cornell/Geneva and NC-140 report it as more precocious than M.7 with the highest cumulative yields in multi-site trials. Recommended early, following Cornell as the breeding program of record per the stated preference order — but note that WSU's more conservative reading is the local one, so expect good rather than spectacular early cropping here. Disease resistance is uncontested across all sources.

vigor_pct: 65-85% of seedling depending on soil and scion; WSU says about two-thirds of standard, rising to three-quarters or more on good soils with vigorous scions, while eastern extension sources say 75-85% of standard (85-100% of seedling)
anchorage: free-standing; very well anchored, needs no support or irrigation once established
disease_notes: Resistant to woolly apple aphid and collar rot, and tolerant of fireblight and crown/root rots. Drought tolerant and, unusually, a good choice for heavy or poorly drained soils — the opposite of EMLA 106 in that respect.
description: Properly MM.111 (Malling-Merton), the most vigorous of the widely used semi-dwarfing stocks, giving a large free-standing tree at roughly two-thirds to full seedling size. It is the traditional choice for unsupported standard-style cider orchards, wide spacing, and difficult, droughty or heavy soils, at the cost of slow bearing — expect a longer wait to first meaningful crop than with any Geneva stock. Pairing it with an already-vigorous scion such as Amere de Berthcourt or Lambrook Pippin will produce a very large tree that is expensive to harvest by hand.
discrepancies: Genuine and unresolved size disagreement between authorities. WSU says about two-thirds of a standard tree (up to three-quarters on good soils); extension.org and Maryland Extension say 75-85% of standard or 85-100% of seedling; Cornell simply calls trees on MM.111 semistandard to standard. Recommended reporting the range 65-85% of seedling with the soil/scion caveat rather than a single number, because the spread reflects real environmental sensitivity rather than one source being wrong — and because a well-drained Olympic Peninsula site with vigorous cider scions sits at the large end of that range. Also a naming caution worth recording: the orchard's label M.111 does not exist as a Malling stock; MM.111 is a Malling-Merton selection, and EMLA 111 is its virus-cleaned clone. Assume MM.111/EMLA 111 is meant. Disease and anchorage traits agree across every source.

vigor_pct: 50-70% of seedling; WSU says half to two-thirds of a standard tree, other extensions say 60-70%, giving roughly a 12-14 ft tree
anchorage: free-standing; excellent anchorage, does not usually need support, and seldom root-suckers
disease_notes: Resistant to woolly apple aphid but EXTREMELY susceptible to Phytophthora collar/crown/root rot. It does not tolerate wet feet and requires genuinely well-drained soil. Only moderately fireblight tolerant. This is the critical constraint for a wet-winter maritime site.
description: The virus-cleaned EMLA clone of MM.106, a semi-dwarfing stock long valued for outstanding precocity, heavy production and good anchorage without a trellis. Its defining flaw is crown rot: widespread collar rot losses followed its 1960s introduction, and WSU explicitly conditions its use on well-drained soil. On good ground it performs excellently — WSU's own Mount Vernon cider trial grew Dabinett, Harry Master's Jersey and Tremlett's (Geneva) on MM.106, so the juice data in this library comes from trees on this stock — but on marginal drainage G.890 is the safer substitute at similar tree size.
discrepancies: Only a minor size spread: WSU says half to two-thirds of a standard tree, extension.org and nurseries say 60-70% at about 12 ft. Recommended the wider 50-70% range since both are university sources and the difference is within normal soil variation. Everything else corroborates cleanly across WSU, extension.org, WVU and two nurseries — notably the crown rot susceptibility, which every source independently flags. Naming note: EMLA 106 is the virus-cleaned clone of MM.106 and the terms are used interchangeably in the sources; no meaningful trait difference is reported between them. Worth recording that WSU's Mount Vernon cider cultivar trial used MM.106 as its standard rootstock, so this stock is well proven for cider varieties in this exact climate — provided drainage is adequate.

vigor_pct: 45-55% of seedling; slightly larger than M.26 by some accounts, about 12% smaller than M.26 EMLA in NC-140 trials
anchorage: needs support; very precocious and heavy cropping, so a trellis or stake should always be used. Moderate suckering.
disease_notes: Highly resistant to fireblight and to Phytophthora crown rot (both confirmed by WSU and Cornell), and tolerant of replant disease. NOT resistant to woolly apple aphid — a common and costly misconception. Also sensitive to latent apple viruses, so it must be grafted only with certified virus-clean scion wood.
description: A Geneva semi-dwarfing rootstock from a 1976 Ottawa 3 x Robusta 5 cross, and among the most precocious semi-dwarfs available. It suits high-density supported cider plantings where early return matters, and its fireblight and crown rot resistance are a real advantage over M.26 and MM.106 in a wet climate. Two cautions dominate its use here: the latent-virus sensitivity makes it a poor match for uncertified scion wood — the likely route for obscure cider varieties like Cimetere or Amere de Berthcourt — and its lack of woolly apple aphid resistance means G.890 is the better choice where that pest is a concern. WSU's Mount Vernon trial grew Puget Spice on M.26 and G.935.
discrepancies: The important one is woolly apple aphid. Because the Geneva program is known for WAA-resistant stocks, general sources and casual summaries often imply all Geneva rootstocks share that trait; Cornell and Adams County Nursery both state explicitly that G.935 is susceptible to woolly apple aphid, unlike G.890. Recommended recording it as NOT resistant — this is the single most consequential correction in the rootstock set, and it should drive stock selection if WAA is present on site. Second conflict: size class. WSU calls G.935 dwarfing while Cornell and the release literature call it semi-dwarfing, and reports vary between slightly larger than M.26 and 12% smaller than M.26 EMLA in NC-140 trials. Recommended 45-55% of seedling, roughly M.26 class, following Cornell — the practical takeaway (needs support either way) is unaffected. Fireblight resistance, crown rot resistance, precocity and latent-virus sensitivity are agreed across all sources.
